NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION) — To prevent or mitigate redox cycling degradation in the Ni-YSZ anode of a planar solid oxide fuel cell, I propose introducing a thin, porous, and redox-stable interfacial barrier layer between the anode and electrolyte. Standard practice uses a Ni-YSZ anode directly bonded to the YSZ electrolyte without such a barrier. My mitigation is a genuine departure because existing SOFC anodes lack an interfacial compliant layer, whereas my approach introduces a dedicated buffer zone to accommodate nickel expansion stresses. The closest existing practice is the use of barrier layers in other electrochemical devices (e.g., ceramic barrier coatings in gas separation membranes), but those are dense and non-porous, whereas my solution is specifically designed as a porous, stress-absorbing interface that maintains gas permeability while blocking nickel migration. This intervention attacks the failure's driving physics by providing a compliant, sacrificial layer that absorbs the strain from nickel re-oxidation expansion, preventing stress buildup at the anode-electrolyte interface.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing physical relation is the stress-strain equation σ = E·ε, where the tensile stress σ at the interface is proportional to the Young's modulus E of the material and the strain ε from nickel expansion. By introducing a compliant layer with a lower effective modulus (E_compliant << E_Ni-YSZ), the strain energy is absorbed within the layer rather than transferred to the brittle electrolyte interface. For a 10% volume change in Ni during re-oxidation (ε ≈ 0.1), a compliant layer with E_compliant ≈ 5 GPa (vs. E_Ni-YSZ ≈ 200 GPa) would reduce interfacial stress by a factor of ~40, from ~2 GPa to ~50 MPa, which is below the typical fracture strength of YSZ (~300 MPa).

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — 
1. Thin (5-20 µm) porous samaria-doped ceria (SDC) interfacial layer, deposited via screen-printing (b) [replaces the direct anode-electrolyte interface]
2. Standard Ni-YSZ anode support (a) [unchanged]
3. Standard YSZ electrolyte (a) [unchanged]
4. Modified anode fabrication procedure: screen-print SDC layer before co-firing (c) [adds one step to existing process]
5. Standard co-firing parameters (750°C, 2 hours) (c) [unchanged]

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — 
- Standard practice: Uses Ni-YSZ anode directly bonded to YSZ electrolyte (no additional components or steps).
- My intervention adds only one standard catalog item (SDC powder for screen-printing) and one procedural step (screen-printing the interfacial layer), both of which are common in SOFC manufacturing. The co-firing temperature and time remain unchanged, and no new equipment is required. The total burden is same-or-lower because screen-printing is already part of SOFC fabrication, and SDC is a standard, procurable material. The intervention does not increase cell package thickness beyond the 2 mm constraint, as the SDC layer is ultra-thin (5-20 µm).

EXECUTABLE TEST — 
Protocol: Fabricate identical SOFC cells with and without the SDC interfacial layer (n=10 per group). Subject both groups to 200 redox cycles (750°C, 1-hour reduction in H2, 1-hour oxidation in air, 30-minute dwell at operating temperature between cycles). Measure power density at 0.7 V after every 20 cycles. Monitor interfacial integrity via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to detect delamination (increase in low-frequency arc). 
Pass/fail threshold: Cells with SDC layer must maintain >0.35 W/cm² power density after 200 cycles, while control cells must show >30% degradation. EIS must show no significant delamination in SDC cells (arc area <5% increase) vs. controls (arc area >20% increase).
Duration: 6 months (for cycling testing).
Kill criterion: If any cell with SDC layer shows >20% power density loss or delamination before 100 cycles, the intervention is falsified.
